title: Closing the Workshop and what the quartet members did next
summary: He recalls padlocking the building, then taking tapes to New York, recording with Zawinul, touring with B.B. King, and the quartet's members scattering without ever reuniting.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: which was half of the group at that time. And it was a long time. I mean, many, many years before I ever played with anybody that gave me the completeness and the fullness of playing with that particular group. In fact, we've never ever had that same setting together again. There have been times when it's been George French, David Lee, Willie T, and myself, or Willie T, David Lee, myself, or Willie T, Joyce Davis, and myself, but not all four of us back together again. As I said before, George French came as George Davis was leaving to go with Dizzy or playing at a place called the Horse Stable that was on Bourbon, and that sort of made the complexion of the quartet change and made us start searching for some new music. As I remember now, the last days of seeing the workshop having to close was something that I did not want to come to grips with and did everything we could to just fight to hold on because there was funding that was promised that was coming, but to remain open for the interim period of time was very, very difficult. So as I recall, when I left the workshop, I don't know the exact date, but I remember putting padlocks on the door knowing that we weren't going to be able to function any longer, not only because of economic problems, but because George and David were leaving to go with Dizzy. Willie and I had other projects that were beginning to happen, and this particular core of dedicated musicians you see, we could have gotten all kinds of guys to come in as long as we were able to pay them scale or above or pay them their particular price to come in and play. But in the case of the group that we had, we were dedicated to making this thing happen when we had money and when we didn't, so it functioned and we played with just as much enthusiasm night after night. But as I remember leaving, I mean, I remember locking that building and I often wondered what happened with some of the things because I left lights, sound system, the mural of the blow-up of train and the sign outside and just, it was like tears in my eyes and leaving this wonderful place that I hoped to resurrect at some point or to get it started again. And many times I'd hoped to get, when I came back and saw the building still vacant, of starting up again and taking it from where we had left off. But the closing of a workshop was a very sad thing because we all loved it so much, and many musicians that heard the music and that played in there still said that they've never quite had a duplicate of that experience. After that, I began to use tapes that I had recorded to go to New York to try and seek record deals that Joe Zavno had recommended that I go and talk to a man named Joel Dorn at Atlantic Records. And he was very impressed with the tapes, but we hadn't recorded on the kind of state-of-the-art equipment that was being used so he could understand the concept. But as a result of that, I wound up doing, being in New York to take care of that and running into Zavno then and was contracted to play on the Zavno date on Atlantic, which was his last date, leaving Cannonball, about to start Weather Report, and could have been something that led into that. But it was a very, very good record. It was the number three record of the year here and the number one record of the year in Europe. And from there, I began to set out on pretty much international travels. Then I stayed in New York for a period of time with wonderful hospitality given to me by Walter Booker and enabled me to get acclimated to New York and get into the New York scene, and some record dates were starting to happen. And record dates were starting to happen, and I took off and went on a road with B.B. King in the hopes of just setting up a financial base to really set myself up in New York, which turned out to be a three-year journey around the world. And David remained with Dizzy Gillespie for a while. Joyce was there. And then David later went on to join Sonny Rollins and work with Sonny Rollins for a number of years. And we would come across each other and in and out of contact with each other during that period of time. But never, as I said before, having all four of us together again or to record again or to put that music together again. And I think Joyce started working Chorus Line, which he worked for almost, from the inception to almost the closing, almost a 20-year period of doing that. And David and I would sometimes meet in New York and hang or play some privately, and I played in all kind of other settings. One record date I did with Buster Williams. But we were all off doing separate kind of ventures and venturing out into new music and trying to find the individual places that we fit. But I think that we also, we always talked about it, man, if we could just get this group back together. Because I've had some very, very profound musical experiences in between that period of time and gone to some very special places while playing. But never, even with some of the very best musicians in the world that I play with in New York and other places and David with Sonny and George with Dizzy and other people, sometimes we talk about this, not anything that we can remember that quite equaled the kind of musical, spiritual, and mental travel that we were able to do together and the kind of teleprathy that happened in the music that we played. And I think that anybody that ever experienced the jazz workshop or experienced that particular music that we played knew that it was something that was very specially sent and something that, no matter how much good music you heard during your life, that you never, ever forget the impact of that experience of the place or the music and the music that we collectively, and sometimes, I'm sure in my playing and David's playing and all of our playing, there's something left over from that that was a very part of the formative period. And there are a few rare recordings around of different things that we've done and we're going to try to do our best to track those down and put something together and maybe put something even together in this series so that you can hear bits and pieces of what was happening there. Yeah.
